item.title: Behind the Curtain: The Trump obliteration
item.description:
Make no mistake: Democrats won by epic, sometimes historic margins across red and blue states, up and down ballots, obliterating almost everything President Trump, and a Republican Party remade wholly in his image, built over the past decade in American politics.

Why it matters: Trump and Republicans are left with a mostly white, mostly old House and Senate minority, confronting a younger, more diverse ascendant Democratic Party with power and margins it hasn't held in 18 years, since the dawn of the Obama era.

The results speak louder than any words we can write:

  • Democrats won Senate races in Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, Ohio, and perhaps Mississippi en route to what could be a 55-seat majority.
  • Democrats won swing districts all across red America, with national average margins of victory of roughly 13 points, according to a New York Times estimate.
  • Texas is now a Democratic state, top to bottom — unthinkable mere months ago. James Talarico crushed Ken Paxton (55% to 43%) like it was Connecticut. State Representative Gina Hinojosa will become the first Democratic governor of Texas in 32 years.
  • Pastor Adam Hamilton is the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas in 94 years.
  • North Carolina looks like a true-blue state after Democrats flipped the Senate seat and likely ousted Rep. Richard Hudson (R-N.C.), chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) — meaning he led the GOP drive to keep the House.
  • North Carolina's congressional delegation could swing from 10R-4D to 5R-9D. Georgia was even worse for Republicans, where they lost all power at the state and U.S. Senate levels.
  • Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) predicted on X that the losses were so widespread, so deep, so severe that Republicans might not "have a shot at Senate control until 2032."

How to think about last night more broadly: This is a 50-50 nation with fast, whiplash shifts in power at the federal level due to persistent discontent with the party in power. So, on one hand, this isn't terribly surprising.

  • On the other, Republican losses were so deep, so wide, so everywhere that it would be foolish to see this as anything but a massive repudiation of Trump, his agenda, his style, his rhetoric and his presidency.

If anything, what's left of the Republican Party is more pro-Trump and less likely to challenge him. His critics, even the timid ones, were ousted long before the general election. So Republicans are left with two more years of riding a very unpopular leader managing a very unpopular war. A trapped, embarrassed Trump is even more unpredictable.

  • Democrats have the numbers to investigate Trump, his family and supporters, and the power to set the agenda in the House and Senate.

The bottom line: Voters nationally said government corruption was a "crucial issue" in their vote for Congress. Democrats will spend months trying to rehab a party that, despite its victory, remains deeply unpopular as a brand. Expect a vigorous fight between Mamdani-like socialists and Schumer-like center-leftists.

  • Top takeaways from Axios' Zachary Basu.

item.title: "What we just witnessed was an AI earthquake": Voters revolt against tech at polls
item.description:
Voters showed deep distrust of the AI race Tuesday, approving dozens of data center moratoriums and electing a raft of candidates who favor slowing a $10 trillion buildout, including in Texas — the epicenter of the boom.

Why it matters: In an election that hinged on an affordability crisis for many Americans, voters made it clear they view Silicon Valley's AI ambitions not as a technological miracle, but as a resource-draining threat to their wallets and communities.

  • The results were a warning shot to some of the nation's wealthiest and most powerful executives, many of whom are already working on ways to build a more palatable version of the revolution they are dead-set on winning.

"What we just witnessed was an AI earthquake," Brad Carson, co-founder of Americans for Responsible Innovation, told Axios. "Voters just sent a clear message that they want rules for AI and data centers."

Driving the news: Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa's surprise victory in the Texas governor's race fundamentally scrambles the math for the AI buildout.

  • Hinojosa campaigned on keeping a moratorium on data center construction in place until the state passes legislation tackling impacts on water, electricity, air and property rights in the legislative session that ends in mid-2027.
  • While most 2027 U.S. data centers expected are already under construction, a hold for more than six months would bring extended delays to Texas, which accounts for 41% of new U.S. capacity in 2028, according to the research firm SemiAnalysis.
  • Democrats won all three of the states that follow Texas for new data center capacity, including Ohio, Georgia and Arizona. The winners in Ohio and Georgia favor restrictive policies, although it's not yet clear how those will take shape.

Between the lines: All told, nearly two-thirds of 2028 data center capacity could face delays, although most political analysts don't see Democrats permanently blocking construction.

What they're saying: A host of candidates and politicos called out AI as one of the most important issues in the blue wave, an important signpost ahead of a momentous 2028 presidential race.

  • Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), a 2028 contender who won reelection by a wide margin, called out "the titans of Silicon Valley" in a victory speech, saying they "dig bunkers for themselves" even as they warn "that the artificial intelligence they're creating risks human extinction."
  • AI had its "official debut" as the biggest issue in American politics, former New York Assemblymember and RAISE Act author Alex Bores told Axios. "AI is reaching into every part of our society and economy and it's now crystal clear it's impacting every part of our politics, too."

By the numbers: The anti-tech sentiment extended far beyond those states.

  • Out of 41 data center measures on the ballot across 10 states, about two dozen proposals designed to restrict or block development appeared to have passed based on initial returns, according to Ballotpedia.
  • Ohio hosted the largest share of those ballot fights, and some votes are still forthcoming, including in Arkansas and North Dakota.

Yes, but: In California, a measure that would've enacted a 5% wealth tax on individuals and trusts with more than $1 billion in assets appeared headed for defeat early Wednesday morning.

  • Proposition 40 faced a well-funded opposition from the state's tech luminaries, as well as prominent Democrats like Gov. Gavin Newsom and Xavier Becerra.

The intrigue: Leaning into AI skepticism proved to be a winning strategy for Democrats in swing districts.

  • Democratic challengers successfully weaponized AI policy, ousting Republicans in Ohio, Wisconsin, Arizona and Pennsylvania.
  • Democratic groups had poured ads into these districts attacking GOP incumbents for a 2025 vote that would've neutered state AI legislation.
  • AI safety advocates won or were poised to win races on Tuesday that will expand their coalition in the new Congress, including Colorado's Manny Rutinel and Minnesota's Matt Little.

The bottom line: For years, tech execs have dictated the terms of a seemingly limitless expansion, but this election proves that the ballot box still reigns supreme.

item.title: Hakeem Jeffries gets the majority of his dreams
item.description:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is set to preside over a commanding Democratic majority after his party swept districts President Trump carried by double digits.

Why it matters: Democrats' landslide win will make it much, much easier for the likely next speaker to secure the gavel without a sweat and ignore the demands of his progressive wing.

  • Rep. Greg Stanton (D-Ariz.), a leader of the center-left New Democrat Coalition, told Axios in an interview Tuesday night that Jeffries "now has the space to utilize his full talents as speaker."
  • The size of Democrats' victory, Stanton said, "allows him to govern without worrying about being leveraged by anyone."

Driving the news: Jeffries is on track to enjoy a majority of dozens of votes, with the New York Times projecting Democrats to win as many as 256 seats to Republicans' 178.

  • Democrats flipped districts where the national parties didn't even spend money, likely unseating Republicans such as Reps. Lauren Boebert and Richard Hudson who were considered safe just months ago.
  • It's a major partisan win for Democrats as a whole, but the party's centrist wing is also hailing the result as a much-needed strategic victory over the left.

Zoom in: Progressives — particularly "The Bloc," a group made up of hard-charging leftists like Darializa Avila Chevalier and Adam Hamawy — had hoped to use a small majority to extract concessions from Jeffries.

  • Many of them have declined to commit to supporting Jeffries as speaker and signaled they would use their votes as leverage force votes on progressive legislation such as Medicare-for-All, defunding ICE and cutting aid to Israel.
  • But the left's strategy is "going to look different from what it would have been with a smaller margin," one incoming House progressive told Axios, noting that "leaders have more flexibility when they have big majorities."
  • Progressives "can't really extract much now [with this] colossal majority," a progressive strategist acknowledged, adding that "we don't have to do this high stakes Jeffries fight."

Between the lines: Stanton noted that most of the incoming Democrats who won in purple and red districts were endorsed by the New Dems.

  • The center-left group is one of Jeffries' most reliable power bases in the caucus.
  • "Every single New Dem incumbent, every single candidate that got our endorsement that's winning tonight — and there's a lot of them — I have full confidence they're going to vote for Hakeem Jeffries as speaker," Stanton said.

Yes, but: Several progressives who spoke to Axios noted that many of the Democrats who won upset victories in deep-red districts on Tuesday ran more as rural and rust belt populists than traditional pro-Israel, pro-business centrists.

  • As Axios reported in October, many Democrats who ran in Trump double-digit seats did so with a message that savaged their own party's leadership as much as the GOP's.
  • An incoming member of the progressive "Bloc," asked if Democrats big margin would make it harder for the left to get their demands met, replied, "Yes, but only if leadership takes the wrong lessons from tonight."
  • "Progressive, populist politics won overwhelmingly and came ridiculously close in places no one expected to see. This kind of margin comes with an expectation that we deliver bold changes," they added.

The bottom line: Progressives are warning Jeffries that he will regret looking at Democrats' massive victory as a green light to govern in increments.

  • "I think there's a clear mandate from voters on what sort of progressive economic agenda they want to see," said Usamah Andrabi, a spokesperson for the left-wing Justice Democrats.

item.title: Blue tsunami breaks MAGA: 5 takeaways from a blowout midterm election
item.description:
President Trump's Republican Party suffered an electoral humiliation Tuesday night that stretched across the battleground map and into some of the deepest-red territory in America.

Why it matters: The 2026 midterms will go down as one of the most sweeping repudiations of a sitting president in modern American history, on a scale reminiscent of the post-Watergate reckoning of 1974.

The big picture: Two years after Trump's comeback appeared to herald a historic political realignment, voters delivered a devastating verdict on his second presidency.

  • Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress, on course to gain as many as 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats — eclipsing their wildest pre-election expectations.
  • The wave swept deep into Republican territory, from Texas and Georgia to both Carolinas, flipping hundreds of legislative seats and delivering Democratic trifectas in the unlikeliest of states.

5 takeaways

1. Texas turns blue: After decades of dashed hopes, Democrats finally conquered the nation's most coveted Republican stronghold — in a landslide so sweeping that even three-term Gov. Greg Abbott was driven from office.

  • Gina Hinojosa became the state's first Latina governor, while James Talarico defeated Trump-backed Ken Paxton to become the first Texas Democrat elected to the Senate since 1988.
  • The Democratic onslaught extended across statewide offices and possibly Texas' House of Representatives, suggesting that the state's political future could be up for grabs after 32 years of GOP dominance.

2. Democrats storm Senate: What once looked like an impossibly difficult map for Democrats gave way to a historic rout, as Republicans watched their 53-seat majority crumble in states Trump carried by double digits.

  • Democrats broke a 94-year losing streak in Kansas, ousted Republicans in Ohio, Iowa and North Carolina, and captured South Carolina for the first time since 1998.
  • In Maine, Democrats finally toppled five-term Sen. Susan Collins after many failed attempts, putting them on course for a 54-seat majority — with Alaska and even Mississippi offering a chance to make it 55 or 56.

3. MAGA coalition collapses: The multiracial, working-class coalition that powered Trump's 2024 comeback fractured spectacularly Tuesday, raising serious questions about the long-term durability of his MAGA movement.

  • AP's nationwide voter survey found roughly 70% of voters under 30 and 60% of Hispanic voters backed Democratic House candidates, amid widespread anger over the economy and the Iran war.
  • In heavily Hispanic Starr County, Texas, which Trump famously flipped in 2024, Talarico led by nearly 60 points — a staggering 75-point reversal from two years prior.

4. GOP House firewall crumbles: Democrats are on course for their largest House majority since 2009, potentially winning as many as 255 seats.

  • Casualties spanned the entire GOP conference, from MAGA firebrands to battle-tested moderates. Even seats redrawn to shield Republicans from a blue wave fell to Democrats, turning Trump's redistricting offensive into a spectacular miscalculation.
  • With control of the House secured, Democrats wasted little time signaling what comes next. Incoming Oversight chair Robert Garcia distilled the party's appetite for investigations into two words: "Lawyer up."

5. 2028's winners and losers: Tuesday's landslide elevated a new generation of Democratic contenders and cast a shadow over Vice President Vance's presidential ambitions.

  • Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, whose race was called 15 minutes after polls closed, immediately vaulted into the top tier of Democratic prospects. Keisha Lance Bottoms' historic victory for governor removed a key obstacle for both Ossoff and Sen. Raphael Warnock: She could appoint a Democrat to fill their seat if either became president.
  • Vance, Trump's presumed political heir, now faces the fallout from a deeply unpopular Iran war and the collapse of a once-in-a-generation coalition he hoped would carry him to the White House.

The bottom line: For a decade, Trump has been the gravitational center of American politics. Tuesday's results suggest that era may finally be drawing to a close.

item.title: Everything you need to know about last night in under 1,000 words
item.description:
It was a drubbing on a scale that neither side saw coming: Democrats pummeled Republicans across the battleground map and into some of the most MAGA-friendly terrain in the country.

Why it matters: The results were an emphatic rejection of Donald Trump's second term in office — and set the stage for two years of corruption investigations and legislative frustration for the lame-duck president.

Here's a rundown of what you need to know about last night's historic GOP beatdown.

The size of the Dem majorities

It was clear early in the night that Democrats would flip the Senate. Few predicted how big their majority would end up.

  • Democrats will have at least 54 Senate seats, and another two — in Alaska and Mississippi — were too close to call early Wednesday.
  • The New York Times projects Democrats will win 257 seats vs. 178 for Republicans — a 79-seat majority. Those numbers could change as more races are called, but in any scenario it will be an astounding majority.

The big surprises

1. Texas turns blue: After decades of dashed hopes, Democrats conquered the nation's most coveted Republican stronghold — in a landslide so sweeping that even three-term Gov. Greg Abbott was driven from office.

  • Gina Hinojosa will be the state's first Latina governor, while James Talarico defeated Trump-backed Ken Paxton to become the first Texas Democrat elected to the Senate since 1988.
  • The Democratic onslaught extended across statewide offices and into the legislature, suggesting that the entire state's political future could be up for grabs after 32 years of GOP dominance.

2. More red-state romps: Democrats broke a 94-year losing streak in Kansas, ousted Republicans in Ohio, Iowa and North Carolina, and captured South Carolina for the first time since 1998.

3. House district reversals. Tennessee's 4th Congressional District race hadn't been called as of the wee hours Wednesday. But the returns were stunning regardless of the outcome.

  • Trump carried the district two years ago by 24 points, and the Democratic candidate, Victoria Broderick, spent just $90,000 on her entire campaign as of Oct. 14. There was no record of her airing a single paid ad.
  • Yet Broderick was leading Rep. Scott DesJarlais by roughly 200 votes. Two years ago, Broderick received just 26.8% of the vote to DesJarlais' 70%.
  • Other House race results were littered with similar red-to-blue 180s from two years ago.

How the pollsters performed

Democrats fretted that polls showing a blue wave were overestimating the party's strength. It turned out polls underestimated the size of the Democratic romp — in some cases by a lot.

  • The midterm polling was "worse than you think," Lakshya Jain, a data and polling expert, wrote last night. "The polls actually missed low on Democrats more than they whiffed on Republicans in 2016. In fact, the national environment is D+13, which is four points more Democratic than the national polling average."

How did the GOP redistricting play work out?

Republicans tried to save their House majority with a bold wave of mid-cycle redistricting. It failed in spectacular fashion on Tuesday.

  • Republicans not only fell short of winning seats in several districts they redrew to favor their candidates, they put some GOP incumbents in danger of losing by spreading their support thin.
  • In Florida, Republicans are set to go 0-for-4 in redistricted seats, and in Texas they're set to narrowly win just one of the five districts they heavily redrew in their favor.
  • The GOP also failed to dislodge Democrats in Ohio and Alabama who they drew into Republican-friendly districts.

MAGA coalition collapse

The multiracial, working-class coalition that powered Trump's 2024 comeback fractured spectacularly Tuesday, raising serious questions about the long-term durability of his MAGA movement.

  • AP's nationwide voter survey found roughly 70% of voters under 30 backed Democratic House candidates, amid widespread anger over the economy and the Iran war.

Hispanic voters swing back

Republicans bet Trump's Latino breakthrough two years ago would create a lasting GOP realignment in Texas and beyond. Tuesday's results exposed how quickly those gains could unravel — and raised new questions about Republicans' coalition heading into 2028.

  • The clearest examples of the Latino shift away from Trump came in Texas counties that Republicans had celebrated as evidence of their growing strength.
  • In heavily Hispanic Starr County, Texas, which Trump famously flipped in 2024, Talarico led by nearly 60 points — a staggering 75-point reversal from two years prior.
  • Democrats are poised to control three congressional seats in Texas' Rio Grande Valley that Trump carried in 2024 — and the margins weren't even close.

The verdict on AI

Voters sent a clear message on Tuesday about AI and data centers: less construction, more regulation.

  • Hinojosa's surprise victory in the Texas governor's race fundamentally scrambles the math for the AI buildout, given the state was expected to host nearly half of new 2028 data center capacity.
  • Democrats won all three of the states that follow Texas for new data center capacity, including Ohio, Georgia and Arizona. The winners in Ohio and Georgia favor restrictive policies, although it's not yet clear how those will take shape.

2028's winners and losers

Tuesday's landslide elevated a new generation of Democratic contenders and cast a shadow over Vice President JD Vance's presidential ambitions.

  • Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, whose race was called 15 minutes after polls closed, immediately vaulted into the top tier of Democratic prospects. Keisha Lance Bottoms' historic victory for governor removed a key obstacle for both Ossoff and Sen. Raphael Warnock: She could appoint a Democrat to fill their seat if either became president.
  • Vance, Trump's presumed political heir, now faces the fallout from a deeply unpopular Iran war and the collapse of a once-in-a-generation coalition.

Maria Curi, Hans Nichols, Zachary Basu, Russell Contreras, Andrew Solender and Mike Zapler contributed.

It was a drubbing on a scale that neither side saw coming: Democrats pummeled Republicans across the battleground map and into some of the most MAGA-friendly terrain in the country.

Why it matters: The results were an emphatic rejection of Donald Trump's second term in office — and set the stage for two years of corruption investigations and legislative frustration for the lame-duck president.

Here's a rundown of what you need to know about last night's historic GOP beatdown.

The size of the Dem majorities

It was clear early in the night that Democrats would flip the Senate. Few predicted how big their majority would end up.

  • Democrats will have at least 54 Senate seats, and another two — in Alaska and Mississippi — were too close to call early Wednesday.
  • The New York Times projects Democrats will win 257 seats vs. 178 for Republicans — a 79-seat majority. Those numbers could change as more races are called, but in any scenario it will be an astounding majority.

The big surprises

1. Texas turns blue: After decades of dashed hopes, Democrats conquered the nation's most coveted Republican stronghold — in a landslide so sweeping that even three-term Gov. Greg Abbott was driven from office.

  • Gina Hinojosa will be the state's first Latina governor, while James Talarico defeated Trump-backed Ken Paxton to become the first Texas Democrat elected to the Senate since 1988.
  • The Democratic onslaught extended across statewide offices and into the legislature, suggesting that the entire state's political future could be up for grabs after 32 years of GOP dominance.

2. More red-state romps: Democrats broke a 94-year losing streak in Kansas, ousted Republicans in Ohio, Iowa and North Carolina, and captured South Carolina for the first time since 1998.

3. House district reversals. Tennessee's 4th Congressional District race hadn't been called as of the wee hours Wednesday. But the returns were stunning regardless of the outcome.

  • Trump carried the district two years ago by 24 points, and the Democratic candidate, Victoria Broderick, spent just $90,000 on her entire campaign as of Oct. 14. There was no record of her airing a single paid ad.
  • Yet Broderick was leading Rep. Scott DesJarlais by roughly 200 votes. Two years ago, Broderick received just 26.8% of the vote to DesJarlais' 70%.
  • Other House race results were littered with similar red-to-blue 180s from two years ago.

How the pollsters performed

Democrats fretted that polls showing a blue wave were overestimating the party's strength. It turned out polls underestimated the size of the Democratic romp — in some cases by a lot.

  • The midterm polling was "worse than you think," Lakshya Jain, a data and polling expert, wrote last night. "The polls actually missed low on Democrats more than they whiffed on Republicans in 2016. In fact, the national environment is D+13, which is four points more Democratic than the national polling average."

  • Republicans not only fell short of winning seats in several districts they redrew to favor their candidates, they put some GOP incumbents in danger of losing by spreading their support thin.

  • The GOP also failed to dislodge Democrats in Ohio and Alabama who they drew into Republican-friendly districts.

MAGA coalition collapse

The multiracial, working-class coalition that powered Trump's 2024 comeback fractured spectacularly Tuesday, raising serious questions about the long-term durability of his MAGA movement.

  • AP's nationwide voter survey found roughly 70% of voters under 30 backed Democratic House candidates, amid widespread anger over the economy and the Iran war.

Republicans bet Trump's Latino breakthrough two years ago would create a lasting GOP realignment in Texas and beyond. Tuesday's results exposed how quickly those gains could unravel — and raised new questions about Republicans' coalition heading into 2028.

item.title: How Texas went Democratic
item.description:
Texas woke up red on Tuesday and went to bed blue.

Why it matters: Just months ago, Democratic campaigns in the MAGA heartland appeared quixotic — obligatory more than realistic.

  • Now those Democratic candidates have swept to power, led by two state representatives from liberal Austin — James Talarico, soon to be seated in the U.S. Senate, and Gina Hinojosa, who will take her place in the new year in the governor's mansion.

Zoom in: The Democratic victories were comprehensive. State Rep. Vikki Goodwin (D-Austin) unseated three-term Republican Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, per the Associated Press.

  • Democrat Nathan Johnson, a state senator from Dallas, defeated Republican Mayes Middleton, state senator from Galveston, in the race for attorney general.

What they're saying: "We shocked the world tonight. With a Texas chip on our shoulder, we showed the world that anything is possible tonight," Hinojosa said.

  • "We just took back Texas," Talarico told his supporters.

What happened: An unpopular president and high gas and grocery prices deep-sixed red-state GOP candidates across the country.

  • But the Texas GOP was further hampered by an unpopular U.S. Senate candidate (even members of his own party impeached him) — Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
  • And Greg Abbott, who had served as governor since 2015, was unwilling to debate his gubernatorial opponent.
  • Meanwhile, the Democrats were disciplined, with Talarico and Hinojosa staying on message about affordability even as their Republican opponents tried to make the race about social issues.

Follow the money: Republicans went down despite a rescue mission from Elon Musk, who gave north of $150 million in support of Paxton's campaign in a single quarter this year — and gave at least $5.5 million to Abbott's campaign this cycle.

The big picture: The Democratic wins have huge implications for the 2028 presidential race.

  • Democrats have proven, after years of flailing, that they could win statewide in Texas, potentially putting the Lone Star State and its 40 electoral votes in play.
  • Political pundits will be wondering: Was this a one-off wave amid a terrible midterm climate for Texas Republicans — or a sign of foundational change?

The bottom line: Fireworks were shooting off in Austin last night, and state agencies so long occupied by the GOP will now be run by Democrats, opening the way for wide policy changes in long-conservative Texas.

item.title: GOP's redistricting firewall pummeled by blue wave
item.description:
Republicans tried to save their House majority with a bold wave of mid-cycle redistricting. It failed in spectacular fashion on Tuesday.

Why it matters: Republicans not only fell short of winning seats in several districts they redrew to favor their candidates, they put some GOP incumbents in danger of losing by spreading their support thin.

  • Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R-Tenn.), who has mostly won landslide reelections since entering Congress in 2010, trailed his Democratic opponent by 200 votes, according to the Tennessee secretary of state's unofficial final results.
  • Republican state legislators carved up his district in an effort to shore up neighboring Republicans, making his district nearly 20 percentage points less GOP-leaning.

State of play: While Republicans succeeded in picking up a Democratic district in Tennessee to make up for that loss, they largely failed to pick up the seats they tried to make reliably Republican in other states.

  • Florida: Republicans are set to go 0-for-4 in redistricted seats, failing to unseat Democratic Reps. Darren Soto, Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz, or capture a new seat that Democrat Pia Dandiya won.
  • Texas: Republicans are set to narrowly win just one of the five districts they redrew heavily in their favor, with Democrats easily hanging onto several Rio Grande Valley and San Antonio-area seats.
  • Ohio: Democratic Reps. Greg Landsman and Marcy Kaptur held on despite Republicans drawing them into more hostile territory.
  • Alabama: Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures is also set for a comfortable win in a district Republicans had planned to fall into their hands.
  • Louisiana: The district of retiring Democrat Rep. Cleo Fields, which Republicans made significantly more GOP-leaning will go to a December runoff between Democrat Patricia Moore and Republican Gabe Firment.

One of the most stunning results of the night was Democrats' multiple apparent victories in North Carolina, where House candidates were boosted by Sen-elect Roy Cooper's strong performance at the top of the ballot.

  • Democrats are on track to flip several seats that were rated as likely or even solidly Republican by Cook Political Report, likely unseating Republican Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore.
  • They are also likely to unseat Rep. Richard Hudson, the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee. Virginia Foxx, who chairs the House Rules Committee, is behind by about 100 votes.
  • In all, the state's House delegation could go from a 10-4 Republican majority to a 9-5 Democratic one.

Between the lines: The North Carolina result is the product of a brutal 2024 gerrymander in which GOP state legislators diluted most solidly Republican districts to draw out several House Democrats.

  • They redistricted again last year, only to put Democratic Rep. Don Davis in more hostile territory.
  • GOP Rep. Greg Murphy — whose district was packed with more Democratic voters to make Davis' seat redder — barely hung on Tuesday night.
  • Former Democratic Rep. Kathy Manning, who was one of the Democrats drawn out in 2024, told Axios that Tuesday's result was "absolutely" a result of GOP redistricting backfiring.

The bottom line: Republicans "tried to break the laws and go against these norms in your massive authoritarian power grab," DNC vice chair Shasti Conrad told Axios.

  • "How did that turn out?"

item.title: WIPEOUT: GOP LOSES HOUSE AND SENATE
item.description:
Republicans lost deep-red Senate seats in South Carolina, Kansas and Texas as well as House seats nationwide, AP projects, giving Democrats control of both chambers of Congress.

Why it matters: President Trump made himself the face of the GOP campaign for control. Now his party is losing all over the map, and he's distancing himself from the outcome.

Data: AP; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios
  • Former President Obama wrote on X: "Tonight, the American people sent a clear message — they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face."

Zoom in: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won election to U.S. Senate from Michigan, AP projects, adding to the Democrats' already rushing blue wave.

  • In Texas, James Talarico secured a history U.S. Senate seat, defeating Trump-backed Republican opponent, Ken Paxton. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott conceded to Democrat Gina Hinojosa in the Texas governor race.
  • In Kansas, Adam Hamilton flipped the country's longest-held Republican Senate seat, ending a 94-year drought.
  • In Maine, Susan Collins conceded to Troy Jackson in the Senate race.
  • In Minnesota, Democrat Peggy Flanagan won election to U.S. Senate, AP projects.
  • In South Carolina, Sen. Darline Graham will lose reelection to Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, AP projects.
  • In Iowa, Democratic nominee Josh Turek defeated Rep. Ashley Hinson to flip the Senate seat vacated by retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, AP projects.
Data: AP; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios

Zoom out: Former Gov. Sherrod Brown (D) defeated Sen. Jon Husted (R) in Ohio, AP projects.

  • Earlier in the night, Democrat Roy Cooper defeated Trump's handpicked candidate, Michael Whatley in North Carolina while Democrat Jon Ossoff won reelection to U.S. Senate in Georgia, AP projects.
  • In North Carolina's 11th House district, Jamie Ager flipped the seat for Democrats. The seat is held by retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards, who ended his reelection bid after the House Ethics Committee recommended he be censured.

Between the lines: The results tonight were a clear national test of Trump's second presidency, following war abroad, economic anxiety at home and sweeping changes in Washington.

  • "I am absolutely willing to accept those results," Trump said in an interview with The New York Times.
  • "We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll, you know, look forward to working with them. We'll probably work something out."

Yes, but: Trump wrote on Truth Social he plans to criticize the candidates that lost. He also posted an image of a red hat with the word, "VETO."

Earlier in the night, Trump raged on social media about the results. He made Fox News the subject of his ire by critiquing Fox's political polling, calling it "a hit job, and every answer is 'BULLSHIT!'"

  • He also texted on-air guests to rage against Jessica Tarlov, a Fox co-host and Democratic strategist he called "DUMB AS A ROCK."
  • This came hours after he criticized multiple Democrat candidates as voters went to the polls.

The intrigue: Tuesday night's results created some historic moments beyond control for Washington and Trump's ire.

  • Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the U.S. Senate after besting former GOP Sen. John Sununu in the New Hampshire race.
  • There will be three Black women serving in the U.S. Senate for the first time in history after Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton won the Senate race in Illinois. She will join Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Delaware) and Angela Alsobrooks (D-Maryland), who became the first two Black women to serve simultaneously in 2025.

What we're hearing: Voters identified the cost of living and government corruption concern as the two top issues in this year's election, according to exit polls from AP.

  • Cost of living skyrocketed thanks to the Iran war and the president's tariff policies. Trump himself was deemed corrupt and dangerous in a poll of registered voters prior to the election.

The bottom line: Republicans have largely given Trump a free hand in Washington since his return to the White House. Democratic control of even one chamber of Congress will open the door to investigations, subpoenas and even more legislative gridlock.

item.title: El-Sayed becomes first Muslim U.S. senator
item.description:
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's closely watched U.S. Senate race, the Associated Press projected. He will become the nation's first Muslim senator.

Why it matters: El-Sayed's win shows how an unapologetically progressive candidate can win in a battleground state President Trump carried just two years ago.

  • The two candidates competed for the seat vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, with Republicans hoping to flip a seat Democrats have held for decades. But the GOP failed in its endeavor — and already lost its Senate majority.
  • The race took a stunning turn in its final days, when Democratic U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost the August primary to El-Sayed, endorsed Rogers.
  • The move sparked furious backlash from Democrats and prompted several of Stevens' staffers, including her chief of staff, to resign.

The big picture: El-Sayed, a former Detroit health director, ran on a progressive platform centered on Medicare for All, taxing billionaires and reducing corporate influence in politics.

  • His victory comes after a contentious Democratic primary and a bitter general election campaign that featured personal attacks over his background, medical credentials and Muslim faith.
  • Rogers, a former congressman and FBI agent who narrowly lost a 2024 Senate bid, sought to portray El-Sayed as too extreme for Michigan. El-Sayed cast Rogers as a Washington insider aligned with Trump.
  • Trump himself escalated the attacks in the final stretch of the race, questioning El-Sayed's loyalty to the U.S. and making unsubstantiated allegations of extremist ties. El-Sayed rejected the accusations.

Between the lines: El-Sayed's win offers progressives a powerful new argument in the Democratic Party's debate over how to win back voters.

Zoom out: Both candidates put affordability at the center of their campaigns but offered sharply different solutions.

  • El-Sayed called for universal health care, tackling medical debt and higher taxes on billionaire wealth.
  • Rogers emphasized tax cuts, expanding domestic manufacturing and more transparent health care prices. He also campaigned on stronger border security and immigration enforcement.

What's next: El-Sayed will arrive in Washington with an ambitious progressive agenda — but turning campaign promises into legislation will be a different challenge.

  • His signature Medicare for All proposal faces steep political obstacles, even with Democrats winning control of the Senate.
  • His victory also gives progressives a new national figure as Democrats begin looking toward the 2028 presidential election.

item.title: The 5 biggest shockers of Democrats' stunning night
item.description:
In red states and blue, Republicans suffered losses on a scale even Democrats would never have dared to dream about 24 hours ago.

Why it matters: Democrats worried that polls showing a blue wave were overestimating the party's strength. It turned out polls underestimated the size of the Democratic romp — by a lot.

The margins Democrats racked up in red states were stunning:

  • Georgia: Sen. Jon Ossoff won reelection by nearly 18 percentage points.
  • North Carolina: Former Gov. Roy Cooper won his Senate race by roughly 19 points.
  • Texas: State Rep. James Talarico cruised to victory by approximately 12 points.

These weren't nail-biters in competitive states. They were landslides in states President Trump carried just two years ago.

1. The Texas trifecta

Democrats won the Texas House, Senate and governor's mansion, giving the party unified control of state government for the first time since 1995.

The sweep came alongside Talarico's double-digit victory in the U.S. Senate race.

Texas, long the GOP's biggest electoral stronghold, delivered Democrats victories up and down the ballot.

2. North Carolina was a bloodbath

The man in charge of steering House Republicans to victory — Rep. Richard Hudson, chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee — lost his own seat.

  • He'll join the ranks of other defeated party leaders — Speaker Tom Foley in 1994 and Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Sean Patrick Maloney in 2022 — who spent so much time trying to build a majority that they failed to protect themselves.
  • The carnage extended across the state. North Carolina's congressional delegation could shift from 10 Republicans and four Democrats to five Republicans and nine Democrats.

3. The ridiculously cheap wins

  • Democrats are leading in districts that received little or no outside spending from the DCCC or House Majority PAC, the party's main House super PAC, according to AdImpact.
  • In North Carolina's 6th, 9th and 13th districts, Missouri's 2nd and Tennessee's 4th, Democratic candidates are on track to win despite receiving little financial support from national Democratic groups.
  • North Carolina's 6th: Democrat Cyril Jefferson didn't spend a dime on advertising, according to AdImpact.
  • Tennessee's 4th: Democrat Victoria Broderick spent just $90,000 on her entire campaign as of Oct. 14, according to her FEC filing. AdImpact has no record of any paid TV advertising.

4. Hispanic voters swung back in South Texas

Democrats are poised to control three congressional seats in the Rio Grande Valley that President Trump carried in 2024 — and the margins weren't even close.

  • Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) was leading Republican Tano Tijerina, 66% to 30%.
  • Democrat Bobby Pulido was leading Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, 62% to 38%.
  • Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas) was leading Republican Eric Flores, 56% to 40%.

The results were a dramatic reversal in a region where Republicans had made significant gains with Hispanic voters during the Trump era.

5. Democrats won deep in Trump country

  • Democrats didn't just flip swing districts — they broke through in some of the reddest corners of the House map.
  • In Tennessee's 4th Congressional District, which Trump carried by 24 points, Broderick was leading Rep. Scott DesJarlais by roughly 200 votes.
  • Two years ago, Broderick received just 26.8% of the vote to DesJarlais' 70%.

The bottom line: The wave didn't discriminate. It washed away good candidates and bad, senators, governors and seasoned Republicans alike.
item.content:encoded:
In red states and blue, Republicans suffered losses on a scale even Democrats would never have dared to dream about 24 hours ago.

Why it matters: Democrats worried that polls showing a blue wave were overestimating the party's strength. It turned out polls underestimated the size of the Democratic romp — by a lot.

The margins Democrats racked up in red states were stunning:

  • Georgia: Sen. Jon Ossoff won reelection by nearly 18 percentage points.
  • North Carolina: Former Gov. Roy Cooper won his Senate race by roughly 19 points.
  • Texas: State Rep. James Talarico cruised to victory by approximately 12 points.

These weren't nail-biters in competitive states. They were landslides in states President Trump carried just two years ago.

1. The Texas trifecta

Democrats won the Texas House, Senate and governor's mansion, giving the party unified control of state government for the first time since 1995.

The sweep came alongside Talarico's double-digit victory in the U.S. Senate race.
